source.author: Quercetan
source.basis: sidenote "Idem responsione ad Aubertum"; text "Quercetan prefers a Syrup of Hellebore"

2.5.1.3-f11.text: Idem responsione ad Aubertum, Veratrum nigrum, alias timidum & periculosum, vini spiritu etiam & oleo commodum sic usui redditur ut etiam pueris tuto administrari possit

translations.literal: The same, in the reply to Aubert: black veratrum, otherwise timid and dangerous, with spirit of wine also and oil is thus rendered fit for use, that it can safely be administered even to boys.
translations.note: 'Idem' refers to Quercetan, who is named in the main text. 'Timidum' is odd when applied to a drug. It is taken here as 'feared, fearsome'; it may be a corruption. 'Veratrum nigrum' is black hellebore.

source.author: Aelianus Montaltus
source.basis: text "Aelianus Montaltus in his exquisite work de morb. capitis, cap. 31 de mel. sets a special receipt of Hellebore of his own"

2.5.1.3-f12.text: ℞ Syrupe de pomis ℥ ii, aquae borag. ℥ iiii, / Ellebori nigri per noctem infusi in ligatura / 6 vel. 8 gr. mane facta collatura exhibe.

translations.note: 'Syrupe' is presumably meant for 'syrupi' (of syrup). 'Ligatura' is taken as a small cloth bag tied up for the infusion. 'Aquae borag.' is expanded as borage water.

source.author: Aelianus Montaltus
source.basis: text "Aelianus Montaltus in his exquisite work de morb. capitis, cap. 31 de mel. sets a special receipt of Hellebore of his own"

translations.text: Take syrup of apples 2 ounces, borage water 4 ounces, / of black hellebore, steeped overnight tied in a bag, / 6 or 8 grains; in the morning strain it and give it.

source.author: Jason Pratensis, after Valescus
source.basis: text "Valescus admires pulvis Hali, and Jason Pratensis after him"

2.5.1.3-f13.text: ℞ Epithymi semunc. lapidis Lazuli, agarici ana ʒ ii, / Scammonii, ʒ i, Chariophillorum numero 20, pulverisentur / Omnia, & ipsius pulveris scrup. 4 singulis septimanis assumat.

translations.note: This is the recipe for 'pulvis Hali' (Hali's powder), which Burton names just before it. Epithyme is dodder growing on thyme, and agaric is the purging larch fungus. Scammony is a purgative resin. 'Chariophillorum' stands for caryophyllorum, which means cloves. 'Semunc.' means half an ounce. 'Singulis septimanis' means 'each week'. It is printed as lines of verse, but it is a prose prescription.

source.author: Jason Pratensis, after Valescus
source.basis: text "Valescus admires pulvis Hali, and Jason Pratensis after him"

translations.text: Take half an ounce of epithyme, of lapis lazuli and agaric 2 drachms each, / of scammony 1 drachm, cloves to the number of 20; let all be powdered, / and of this powder let him take 4 scruples every week.

translations.note: Chariophillorum is read as caryophyllorum (cloves or clove-pinks); the sense is uncertain. Epithymum is dodder of thyme. 'Numero 20' means twenty in number. 'Assumat' is subjunctive, 'let him take'.
translations.text: Take half an ounce of epithyme, of lapis lazuli and agaric 2 drachms each, of scammony 1 drachm, 20 clove-pinks; let all be powdered, and let him take 4 scruples of this powder every week.

translations.note: Epithyme is dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant, much used as a purge against melancholy. Burton's text does not say whose powder this is. In context it is probably the powder taken with the egg remedy he has just described.

translations.note: The name of a compound medicine, kept as a name. Diacatholicon was a gentle laxative electuary; the name is Greek for 'made of the universal (remedy)', from katholikon, a cure-all. It contained senna, cassia, tamarinds and similar ingredients.
Short for lapis lazuli. Burton's phrase 'of Lapis Armenus and Lazuli' means 'of Armenian stone and lapis lazuli'. Both stones were used in purging pills against melancholy.
The name of a compound medicine, kept as a name. Diasenna was an electuary or confection made with senna (dia- means 'made of'). It was used as a purge.
Pil. is short for pilulae. The name of a standard compound purging pill in the old pharmacopoeias.
